2027-03-28.title: Easter Sunday: the Resurrection of our Lord (Uyirppu)
2027-03-28.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)

Hannah's song: rejoice in the Lord
2027-03-28.alt: Easter Sunday, the feast of feasts. The Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta) begins and lasts seven weeks, until Pentecost. The calendar lists two Gospel passages (Matthew 28:1–6 and John 20:1–18); verify locally which is read at the night service and which at the Qurbana of the day. The fifty days of the Great Fast end with the Resurrection Qurbana.
2027-03-28.verse: He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.
theo: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.” The first words the Church hears on Easter are a summons to a city sitting in darkness. Isaiah speaks to a Jerusalem that has been ruined and emptied: “For darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will appear over you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn.” The prophet sees sons and daughters coming home from far away, the wealth of the nations streaming in, camels from Midian and Sheba bringing gold and frankincense, flocks offered on God's altar. On Easter morning the prophecy finds its true meaning. The light that has come is not a sunrise over a city but a Person risen from the dead. The Syro-Malabar Church celebrates the Uyirppu in the night or before dawn precisely for this reason: the darkness of the church is broken by light, and the people who sat in the shadow of death see the glory of the Lord. Every candle in our hands this night is a small fulfilment of Isaiah: nations coming to the light, and the sons and daughters of the Church gathered from everywhere, from Kerala to the farthest diaspora, singing the same Alleluia.

Then the Church sings with Hannah. She was the barren wife who wept in the temple, mocked by her rival, misunderstood even by the priest. God gave her a son, Samuel, and she poured out her joy: “My heart exults in the LORD; my strength is exalted in my God.” Her song is a song of reversals: the bows of the mighty are broken, the hungry are fed, the barren woman bears seven. And at its centre is a line that only Easter fully explains: “The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.” “He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes.” Mary of Nazareth would echo this song in her Magnificat. On Easter God does the greatest reversal of all: the one who was condemned is vindicated, the one laid in the dust of the tomb is raised, the crucified is made Lord. Paul draws the consequence for us: we who were baptised into his death are to live as people raised from the dead. “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.” “No longer present your members to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life.” “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.” Easter is not only something that happened to Jesus; it is something that has happened to us.

The Gospels tell the morning in two voices. In Matthew the women come to see the tomb; there is a great earthquake; an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it, and the guards become like dead men. The angel says: “Do not be afraid; I know that you are looking for Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.” In John it is still dark when Mary Magdalene comes and finds the stone removed. She runs to Peter and the beloved disciple; they race to the tomb, and the other disciple “saw and believed”, though he saw only the linen wrappings lying there and the cloth rolled up in a place by itself. Then the most tender scene of all. Mary stays outside weeping. She does not recognise Jesus and thinks he is the gardener. He calls her by name: “Mary!” And she turns and says, “Rabbouni!” The Risen Lord is not a ghost or a memory or an idea; he is the same Jesus who knows his own by name, risen in his own body, the body that bore the wounds. He sends her as the first messenger of Easter: “Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord’.” The Church has called her the apostle to the apostles. The Resurrection is a real event in history, witnessed by many: an empty tomb, a stone rolled away, and above all meetings with the living Lord. It is also more than history: Christ has passed through death into a new life in which he will never die again, and he draws us with him.

How a family can follow the Uyirppu, step by step (the order and hours differ between dioceses; follow your parish). First, the gathering in darkness: late on Saturday night or in the early hours of Sunday the people gather in the church, often with the lights off, holding unlit candles. Second, the proclamation: the priest announces the Resurrection of the Lord. In many parishes the curtain is drawn back or the image of the Risen Christ is lifted from the tomb where the crucified Lord was laid on Friday, and the light spreads from candle to candle until the whole church shines. Third, the bells and the hymn of glory: the bells, silent since Pesaha, ring out, and the people sing the hymns of the Resurrection. Fourth, the procession: the image of the Risen Lord is carried around the church with candles, crosses and umbrellas, and the people follow singing; in some places it is accompanied by the joyful sound of bells and fireworks. Fifth, the Holy Qurbana of the Resurrection, the first Qurbana of Easter, in which we receive the living Body of the risen Lord. Sixth, the greeting and the meal: people greet one another with the Easter joy, and families go home to break the fifty days' fast together, often with appam and stew or meat curry, and to share with the poor. The fast was never an end in itself; its whole purpose was to bring us here, to the empty tomb and the living Lord. A practical word: take a moment at home to bless the table with the water blessed on Great Saturday, and let the head of the family say: Christ is risen. And let all answer: He is truly risen.
conn: “Arise, shine; for your light has come” (Isaiah 60:1); Christ says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and the women come to the tomb “as the first day of the week was dawning” (Matthew 28:1).
Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1–10) is echoed in Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55); both sing of a God who lifts up the lowly. At Easter he lifts up his Son from the dust of death.
Adam and Eve lost life in a garden (Genesis 3:23–24); Jesus is buried and rises in a garden (John 19:41), and Mary thinks he is the gardener (John 20:15).
“I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1); the good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3), and Mary knows him when he says “Mary!” (John 20:16).
Jesus promised the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:40); “on the third day” he is raised, “in accordance with the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4).
The day the LORD has made.
“This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 118:24): the psalm of the rejected stone becomes the song of Easter.
altar: The Resurrection is the heart of the Holy Qurbana. We do not receive a dead memory but the living Lord, his true Body and Blood, risen and glorified. The Qurbana is the Easter meal of the Church, celebrated every Sunday because every Sunday is a little Easter.
As Mary Magdalene was called by name at the tomb, so each of us is called by name at the altar to receive the Body of Christ. The Amen we say at Communion is our ‘Rabbouni’.

live: Greet every family member and friend today with the words: Christ is risen!
Share the Easter meal with the whole family, and invite or send food to someone who is alone.
Choose one sin you will no longer ‘present your members’ to, and replace it with a work of grace (Romans 6:13).
Make Easter last: pray the ‘Queen of Heaven’ (Regina Caeli) at noon each day until Pentecost.
fathers: St John Chrysostom, Paschal homily (in substance)

Let no one fear death, for the death of the Saviour has set us free. He has destroyed it by enduring it. Hell took a body and met God face to face; it took earth and encountered heaven. O death, where is your sting? O hell, where is your victory? Christ is risen, and you are overthrown; Christ is risen, and life reigns.

Blessed is he who was crucified, who came down from the Cross and went down to Sheol, and rose and gathered us into his Church. The dead heard his voice in Sheol, and Sheol vomited them out, as the sea gave back Jonah. Glory to the Hidden One who became visible, and to the Dead One who came to life.
magis: The Resurrection of Jesus is the crowning truth of our faith; it is a real event with historically verifiable manifestations.
The empty tomb is the first step towards recognising the Resurrection; it is not in itself a direct proof.
The risen Jesus is the same one who suffered; his body is real but glorified, no longer bound to space and time. The Resurrection is not a return to earthly life.
The Resurrection opens for us the way to a new life: justification restores us to God's grace, and Christ is the principle and source of our future resurrection.
Easter is not simply one feast among others but the Feast of feasts.
saints: Monday 29 March to Saturday 3 April: the first week of Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. Friday 2 April: in the East Syriac tradition, the feast of all the saints (verify locally). Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the confession of St Thomas: “My Lord and my God!” The Annunciation, which fell on Pesaha this year, is kept as the Syro-Malabar Ordo directs (verify locally).
2027-03-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are risen from the dead, and death no longer has dominion over you. Glory to you! You broke the bars of Sheol, you rolled away the stone, and you called Mary by her name in the garden. Call us by name, too, and turn our weeping into joy. Make us dead to sin and alive to God; let us walk in newness of life as children of the light. Fill your Church in every land with the gladness of this day, and bring us at last, with all the saints, to the feast that has no end. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-03-28.question: Have I heard the Risen Lord call me by name, and to whom will I go and say: I have seen the Lord?
kidsaint: She loved Jesus very much and stayed near his cross. On Easter morning she went to his tomb crying, and Jesus called her by her name: “Mary!” She was the first to tell the apostles, “I have seen the Lord!” Lesson: Jesus knows your name too, and wants you to tell others about him!
2027-03-28.special: Easter Sunday: the Resurrection of our Lord. The Season of the Resurrection begins. The Great Fast ends.
term: The Syriac word for Resurrection, which gives its name to the Season of the Resurrection in the Syro-Malabar calendar: the seven weeks from Easter to Pentecost, a time of joy in the new life given by the Risen Christ.

family.explain: On Easter morning Mary Magdalene was crying at Jesus' tomb, because his body was gone. Then someone said her name: “Mary!” It was Jesus! He was alive! He had really died, and now he is risen and will never die again. Mary ran to tell the disciples: “I have seen the Lord!” Today we are happy because Jesus is alive and with us always.
family.intention: We thank Jesus for rising from the dead, and we pray for everyone who is sad today, that they may know he is alive.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can we tell today that Jesus is alive, and how?”

illus: A Syro-Malabar family in Mississauga had lost their father in the winter. On Easter night the mother almost stayed home: she could not bear the crowds and the singing. Her teenage daughter said, “Amma, Appa would want us there.” They sat in the back row in the dark. When the priest proclaimed the Resurrection and the lights came on, the little boy beside them, a stranger, turned and handed the mother his own candle, already lit. She said afterwards that it was the first moment since the funeral when she believed, not just knew, that her husband's story did not end in the cemetery. The flame passed from a child she did not know was the Easter Gospel for her.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, risen and living, we gather in your joy. Call each of us by name. Amen. Alleluia!
share: Arise, shine; for your light has come (Isaiah 60:1). What darkness in my life is the Risen Lord shining into?
He raises up the poor from the dust (1 Samuel 2:8). Where has God lifted me up?
Consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God (Romans 6:11). What will I leave behind in the tomb?
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” (John 20:16). Have I heard him call my name?

interc: For the Church throughout the world, that she may proclaim the Resurrection with joy and courage.
For the newly baptised, that they may live as children of the light.
For those who mourn this Easter, that the Risen Lord may call them by name.
For Christians who suffer persecution, that the hope of the Resurrection may strengthen them.
For our families, that our homes may be full of the peace and joy of the Risen Lord.
pm.close: Father, you raised your Son from the dead and opened for us the gate of eternal life. Make us witnesses of his Resurrection in word and deed, until we see him face to face. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, Christ is risen! He is truly risen! This night the darkness of the church was broken by light, and we heard Isaiah say: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.” The light that has come is not a sunrise. It is a Person. Jesus is alive.

We sang with Hannah: “The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.” She sang it for a child born to a barren woman. We sing it for the Son raised from the tomb. God has done the greatest reversal of all: the condemned is vindicated, the crucified is Lord.

The women came to the tomb in the dark. The stone was rolled away, and the angel said: “He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.” The tomb is empty, not because someone took his body, but because he is risen in his body, the same body that bore the wounds.

And Mary Magdalene, weeping in the garden, thought he was the gardener. Then he said her name: “Mary!” And she knew him. That is Easter: not an idea, not a memory, but a living Lord who knows his own by name.

Paul tells us what this means: “consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.” Easter happened to Jesus, and through Baptism it has happened to us. Let us not go back to the tomb we have left. Let us walk in newness of life.

Today we break the fast. Let us do it with joy, and let no one be alone at Easter: share your table, visit the lonely, forgive the one who hurt you. And like Mary Magdalene, let us go and tell someone: I have seen the Lord. Christ is risen! Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus is alive! On Easter morning his tomb was empty, because God raised him from the dead.
Mary Magdalene was crying, and Jesus called her by her name: ‘Mary!’ Jesus knows your name too!
Today let's say to everyone we meet: ‘Jesus is risen! Alleluia!’
